title: The Shed on the Rue Vauquelin: Warsaw, Paris, and the Two Elements
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Freta Street, the fifth child
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'. Coordinate taken from OpenStreetMap for Freta 16, the house now holding the Maria Skłodowska-Curie Museum; the research pool's first figure, 52.2508/21.0069, was about 130 m off and is corrected here.
stops.campa: In a house on Freta Street in the New Town of Warsaw, a fifth child is born to two schoolteachers, Władysław and Bronisława Skłodowski, and is named Maria Salomea. The city is not the capital of a country. Congress Poland is a province of the Russian Empire, its schools teach in Russian, and the father who teaches mathematics and physics will lose his posts and his salary before his daughter is grown. He brings the instruments home from a laboratory the authorities have closed, and the children grow up looking at them behind glass.
stops.quote: My family is of Polish origin, and my name is Marie Sklodowska.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, 'Autobiographical Notes,' Chapter I, appended to Pierre Curie (Macmillan, 1923), Wikisource
suggested_refs: The house at 16 Freta Street, destroyed in the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, rebuilt after the war, and opened in 1967 as the Maria Skłodowska-Curie Museum

stops.name: The Russian gymnasium, the gold medal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the graduation date and the medal (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'). The two family deaths are attested to the years 1876 and 1878 only. Jadwiga Sikorska's boarding school is a reconstruction from the dossier chronology; the pin is the gymnasium, not the school.
stops.campa: She is eight when her sister Zofia dies of typhus caught from a boarder the family has taken in for money, and ten when her mother dies of tuberculosis. Between the two deaths she is a pupil at Jadwiga Sikorska's private boarding school. No university in the Russian partition will admit a woman, so the end of school is the end of her education. She finishes at a Russian government gymnasium whose curriculum is built to keep Polish history and the Polish language out of the room, and on the twelfth of June she takes its gold medal. She is fifteen years old.
suggested_refs: The Russian-language gymnasium curriculum of Congress Poland after the January Uprising
sources: research dossier, Chronological Life History (22 Aug 2026)

stops.name: Warsaw, the university with no building
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Flying University attendance is attested (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie') but not to a month; 1885 is the dossier's year. The pin is a general Warsaw coordinate, since the classes had no fixed address by design. The pact between the sisters is standard biography, carried here as tradition rather than as a documented agreement.
stops.campa: She enrolls instead in an institution that owns nothing. The Uniwersytet Latający, the Flying University, shifts its classes from one apartment to the next to stay ahead of the Russian police, teaches in Polish, admits women, and confers no degree at the end. She reads there with her elder sister Bronisława, and the two settle a bargain between them: Maria will earn and send money while Bronisława qualifies as a doctor in Paris, and Bronisława, qualified, will pay for Maria's turn. Bronisława leaves first.
suggested_refs: The Flying University of Warsaw, clandestine and itinerant, 1882-1905

stops.name: Szczuki, the governess and the mathematician's son
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from standard biography (Quinn, Ogilvie) as synthesized in the dossier; the year 1886 and the refusal of the match are consistently reported, the romantic detail is not documented. Coordinates corrected to Szczuki in gmina Płoniawy-Bramura, Mazovia; the pool's 53.1167/20.3667 lay some 46 km away.
stops.campa: For three years she keeps her side of the bargain as a governess in the country north of Warsaw, in the house of the Żorawski family at Szczuki, teaching their children and sending the wages to Paris. She falls in love with the eldest son, Kazimierz, who is studying mathematics. His parents refuse the match on the plainest of grounds: their son does not marry a poor girl employed in his own house. He does not defy them. She does not leave the post either, and the household goes on as before for two more years.
suggested_refs: The Żorawski estate at Szczuki, powiat makowski, Mazovia
sources: research dossier, synthesis of Quinn and Ogilvie

stops.name: Krakowskie Przedmieście 66, the museum that is a laboratory
stops.date_confidence: attested for the training and the cousin (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'), dated to the year only. Coordinate corrected from OpenStreetMap for Krakowskie Przedmieście 66; the pool's 52.2394/21.0158 was about 700 m south.
stops.campa: Back in Warsaw she is finally let near an experiment. The Museum of Industry and Agriculture on Krakowskie Przedmieście is a museum in name, chosen because the Russian authorities do not inspect museums, and in its rooms she is taught chemical analysis by her cousin Józef Boguski, who was once an assistant to Mendeleev in Saint Petersburg. She is twenty-three and has never handled apparatus before. In the following year Bronisława, now a physician in Paris, sends for her.
suggested_refs: The Museum of Industry and Agriculture, Warsaw, and its concealed teaching laboratory

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the name changed at the register
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1891 (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'); she arrived in the autumn, exact day not in the pool, so the date defaults to 01-01. Coordinate corrected to the Sorbonne at 47 rue des Écoles; the pool's 48.8462/2.3444 is the latitude of the Panthéon, some 380 m away, and the same error recurred four times in the source material.
stops.campa: She crosses Europe in a fourth-class carriage with a folding chair and enters her name in the register of the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Paris: Marie Skłodowska. The French form of the name is adopted here, on paper, at the age of twenty-three, and she will sign it for the rest of her life. Nobody in this country has stopped her from studying physics. Her Polish schooling, though, has left her behind in mathematics, and the first year goes on catching up. Of the roughly two thousand students in the faculty, twenty-three are women.
suggested_refs: The matriculation registers of the Faculty of Sciences, University of Paris, autumn 1891

stops.name: The Latin Quarter, the unheated room
stops.date_confidence: attested as an episode, not as an address: the exact street of the garret is not documented, and the pin locates the Latin Quarter generally. Dated 1892 as the middle of the 1892-1894 period given in the dossier.
stops.campa: She leaves her sister's flat, where the doctor's household is loud and the evenings are Polish, and rents a room of her own near the schools. There is no heat, and no light once the oil runs out, and the water comes up the stairs by hand. She is not poor by accident: she has calculated what she can spend and how many hours it buys her at the bench. So she lives on bread, butter, and tea, and faints in the laboratory more than once. In winter she piles every garment she owns onto the bed and sleeps under all of them.
stops.quote: It was like a new world opened to me, the world of science, which I was at last permitted to know in all liberty.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, 'Autobiographical Notes,' Chapter I, Wikisource
suggested_refs: Ève Curie, Madame Curie (1937), for the garret years and their later legend

stops.name: The Sorbonne, first in the licence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1893 and 1894 respectively (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'); month and day not in the pool. The Lippmann commission on the magnetic properties of steels is attested in the dossier without a precise date.
stops.campa: She places first in the licence in physical sciences, ahead of every French student in the hall, two years after arriving with insufficient mathematics. The following year she places second in the licence in mathematical sciences. Gabriel Lippmann then finds her paid work: a commission from the Society for the Encouragement of National Industry on the magnetic properties of steels. It is a problem in measurement, and the apparatus it wants will not fit in the space Lippmann has to give her. She begins asking around Paris for a room.
suggested_refs: Marie Skłodowska's study of the magnetic properties of tempered steels, commissioned 1894

stops.name: Rue Vauquelin, the introduction
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1894, day not recorded in the pool. The introduction by the Polish physicist Józef Wierusz-Kowalski is attested (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie').
stops.campa: A Polish physicist visiting Paris, Józef Wierusz-Kowalski, hears that she is looking for laboratory space and brings her to a man who might have some. Pierre Curie is thirty-five and chief of laboratory at the municipal school of industrial physics and chemistry on the rue Vauquelin. He discovered piezoelectricity with his brother years ago and holds neither a chair nor a doctorate, and nobody at the Sorbonne can say what he wants. He has no room to spare. They talk about crystals and about the sciences in Poland.
suggested_refs: The École municipale de physique et de chimie industrielles, rue Vauquelin, Paris
sources: ESPCI Paris institutional history, via the research dossier

stops.name: Sceaux, the civil marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'). The pool's place name paired a town hall with a church; the ceremony was expressly civil, with no religious service, so the pin and the name are the mairie alone.
stops.campa: They marry at the town hall of Sceaux, where Pierre's family lives. There is no church and no white dress: she is married in a dark blue cotton suit that will afterwards serve as her laboratory coat, because she cannot afford two garments. With the money given them by relatives they buy two bicycles and ride out of Paris for a honeymoon of no fixed route, sleeping where the road ends each evening. She is twenty-seven and has been in France four years. She has told her family in Warsaw that she will be coming home.
stops.quote: With my marriage there began for me a new existence entirely different from the solitary life that I had known during the preceding years.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, 'Autobiographical Notes,' Chapter II, Wikisource
suggested_refs: The mairie of Sceaux, Hauts-de-Seine, 26 July 1895

segments.name: The Shed on the Rue Vauquelin

stops.name: Rue Vauquelin, the birth of Irene and the choice of a subject
stops.date_confidence: attested for Irène Curie's birth on 12 September 1897 and for the choice of Becquerel's uranium rays as a thesis subject (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'). The pin is the school where the work was done, not the house where the child was born.
stops.campa: A daughter, Irène, is born in September. Two months later her mother is looking for a doctoral subject and takes the one nobody wants: the faint rays Henri Becquerel found coming out of uranium salts the year before, which almost no one has followed up because there seems to be nothing there to follow. She measures them with Pierre's electrometer and the piezoelectric quartz he and his brother built, and finds that the emission is proportional to the quantity of uranium and indifferent to everything else. Heat does not change it. Chemistry does not change it.
stops.quote: But first of all in our life was our scientific work.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, 'Autobiographical Notes,' Chapter II, Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Curie electrometer and piezoelectric quartz balance, Musée Curie, Paris

stops.name: The shed, polonium
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1898 (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'); the eighteenth is the date the dossier and the geography lens both carry for the announcement.
stops.campa: Pitchblende from the Bohemian mines is more active than the uranium it contains, which can only mean that something else is in it. In a disused dissecting shed in the courtyard, under a leaking glass roof and with no ventilation, she boils and precipitates the ore fraction by fraction and follows the activity wherever it goes. In July she and Pierre announce a new element concentrated in the bismuth fraction. She names it polonium, after a country that at that moment appears on no map of Europe.
suggested_refs: The Curies' July 1898 note to the Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences announcing polonium

stops.name: The shed, radium
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'), announced with Pierre Curie and Gustave Bémont on 26 December 1898.
stops.campa: In December, with Gustave Bémont, they announce a second element, in the barium fraction this time, radiant enough to fog a photographic plate through paper and to glow faintly in the dark. They call it radium. They have not seen it, weighed it, or held it; they have inferred it from a spectral line and a number on a dial. The chemists want a sample. Producing one will take four years of hauling sacks of Bohemian mine tailings into the courtyard and stirring boiling vats with an iron rod nearly as tall as she is.
stops.quote: We thought it would be done in several weeks or months, but it was not so. It took many years of hard work to finish that task.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, 'The Discovery of Radium' (Vassar College lecture, 1921), Wikisource
suggested_refs: The December 1898 note announcing radium, signed by Pierre Curie, Marie Curie, and Gustave Bémont
sources: Marie Curie, 'The Discovery of Radium' (1921), Wikisource

stops.name: Sèvres, the first woman at the lectern
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1900 in the dossier's Chronological Life History; month and day not recorded. She had passed the agrégation in 1896, which the pool carries as a reconstruction rather than a documented certificate.
stops.campa: She takes a teaching post at the École normale supérieure de jeunes filles at Sèvres, the training college for the women who will teach France's girls, and is the first woman ever to lecture there. The salary is the reason: the shed consumes money and the ore has to be bought. She travels out to Sèvres by train and back again, teaches physics to future schoolmistresses, and returns to the courtyard in the evening to go on stirring. Her students report that she makes them do the experiments themselves.
suggested_refs: The École normale supérieure de jeunes filles, Sèvres, and its physics teaching under Marie Curie

stops.name: The shed, the decigram and the patent refused
stops.date_confidence: attested as a result of the 1898-1902 shed work; the pool dates the shed period 1898-1902 without a day for the decigram, so the date defaults to 01-01 of the closing year. The refusal to patent is attested in Marie Curie's own words.
stops.campa: After four years she has one decigram of radium chloride, refined from tons of residue, and an atomic weight for it. Industry is already interested: radium will be sold by the gram for cancer therapy and, for a while, for face cream and drinking water. The Curies publish the extraction process in full, take out no patent, and reserve no share of any industrial exploitation. They are not wealthy and they know exactly what they are declining. Two decades later, writing it down, she begins the sentence with a concession and ends it by saying they were right.
stops.quote: But we now know that there is not even one part of radium in a million parts of good ore.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, 'The Discovery of Radium' (Vassar College lecture, 1921), Wikisource
suggested_refs: Marie Curie, 'Autobiographical Notes,' Chapter III, on the decision not to patent: 'Yet, I still believe that we have done right.'
sources: Marie Curie, 'Autobiographical Notes,' Chapter III, Wikisource

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the thesis defended
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1903 (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'); the twenty-fifth is the day given in the geography lens and the dossier's Works section. Coordinate corrected to the Sorbonne proper.
stops.campa: She defends Recherches sur les substances radioactives before the faculty. The examiners tell her the work is the greatest single contribution ever made to science by a doctoral thesis. She is the first woman in France to hold a doctorate in physics. That evening Ernest Rutherford, in Paris and invited to dinner, walks out into the garden with the Curies. Pierre takes from his waistcoat pocket a tube of radium solution in zinc sulphide, glowing well enough to see by. By that light Rutherford notices that Pierre's fingers are inflamed and cannot hold the tube steadily.
suggested_refs: Marie Curie, Recherches sur les substances radioactives (thesis, Paris, 1903)

stops.name: The Royal Institution, the lecture she is not allowed to give
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to venue and day. Wikipedia, 'Pierre Curie', attests the Royal Society's 1903 invitation to London, that Marie Curie was not permitted to deliver the discourse herself, and that Lord Kelvin sat beside her while Pierre spoke; the Davy Medal followed later in 1903. The Royal Institution address at 21 Albemarle Street is the traditional venue for the discourse and is not independently confirmed for this occasion. The pool's 51.5074/-0.142 was about 220 m off.
stops.campa: The Royal Society brings the Curies to London to present the radium work. Marie Curie is not permitted to deliver the lecture; a woman does not speak from that lectern. She sits in the audience while Pierre reads out the results of the four years in the courtyard, and Lord Kelvin, seventy-nine years old and the most eminent physicist in the room, takes the seat next to hers. The Davy Medal comes to them both later in the year. The diamonds she wears that evening are borrowed, and her hands are cracked and scarred from the ore.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society's Davy Medal, awarded jointly to Pierre and Marie Curie in 1903

stops.name: Paris, the prize and the second daughter
stops.date_confidence: attested for the December 1903 award of the Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with Henri Becquerel (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'), and for Ève Curie's birth on 6 December 1904. Neither Curie travelled to Stockholm in 1903; the lecture was given by Pierre on 6 June 1905 and is folded into this stop rather than staged separately.
stops.campa: The Nobel Committee proposes the physics prize to Becquerel and Pierre Curie alone. Pierre is warned in advance by a sympathetic member and answers that he will not accept it unless Marie Curie is named with him. Half the prize is divided between the two of them. Neither travels to Stockholm: they are ill, they are exhausted, and the press has arrived at the door with photographers who want the daughter and the cat in the picture. A second daughter, Ève, is born the following December. Pierre delivers the Nobel lecture in Stockholm on the sixth of June, 1905, and she sits in the hall.
suggested_refs: Pierre Curie's Nobel lecture, 'Radioactive Substances, Especially Radium,' Stockholm, 6 June 1905

stops.name: Rue Lhomond, the Curies say no
stops.date_confidence: attested in loie_fuller.journey.json, which places the refusal at a Paris laboratory address reconstructed as Rue Lhomond and dates it 1904-01-01. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from that file. The later legend that the Curies handed Fuller radium which burned her hands is flagged there as unattested.
stops.campa: The American dancer Loïe Fuller, who has built an entire art out of light thrown onto moving silk, writes to the Curies proposing a costume treated with radium: butterfly wings that would glow on a dark stage. They refuse. There is a decigram of radium in the world, it burns what it touches, and they will not lend the name to a theatre either. Fuller makes the dance anyway, out of the phosphorescent salts she already knows how to handle. She remains a friend of Marie Curie's for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: loie_fuller.journey.json, stop 'Rue Lhomond, the Curies say no'
Wikipedia, 'Loïe Fuller', on the scientists and artists her work drew

stops.name: Rue Dauphine, the rain
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'; dossier, 1904-1906). Marie Curie was not present: she was out of Paris and was told on her return. The stop is hers because the street is where her life divides.
stops.campa: Pierre Curie steps into the rue Dauphine in heavy rain, behind a cab, and is struck by a horse-drawn wagon carrying military uniforms. A rear wheel passes over his skull. He is forty-six, and he had been ill for months with pains in his legs and hands that nobody yet connects to the tubes in his waistcoat pocket. Marie Curie is away when it happens. She is handed the news in the hall of her own house, does not speak for some time, and then asks how it happened, and then asks it again.
stops.quote: I shall not attempt to describe the grief of the family left by Pierre Curie.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, Pierre Curie, Chapter VII (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg, Macmillan, 1923), Wikisource
suggested_refs: Marie Curie's mourning journal, addressed to Pierre, kept from April 1906

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the first lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested for 5 November 1906 by pl.wikipedia, 'Maria Skłodowska-Curie' ('Pierwszy wykład prowadziła 5 listopada 1906 r.'). The research pool's chronology lens gave 13 May 1906 for the same event, conflating two things: 13 May is the date the faculty decided to keep Pierre's chair and offer it to her. The contradiction is left standing in the report and resolved here in favour of the Polish source, which dates the lecture itself.
stops.campa: The faculty votes in May to keep Pierre's chair and give it to his widow. On the fifth of November she stands up in the lecture hall, which is full, with a crowd in the street outside that includes people who have never attended a physics lecture in their lives. There is no memorial preface and no thanks to anybody. She opens at the sentence in the syllabus where Pierre Curie stopped, on the progress of physics in the last ten years, and lectures for the allotted time. She is the first woman ever to teach at the Sorbonne.
stops.quote: I accepted this heavy heritage, in the hope that I might build up some day, in his memory, a laboratory worthy of him, which he had never had, but where others would be able to work to develop his idea.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, Pierre Curie, Chapter VII, Wikisource
suggested_refs: Marie Curie, ed., Oeuvres de Pierre Curie (Paris, 1908), with her preface

stops.name: Meudon, the visit arranged by Fuller
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and weak. The dossier cites correspondence in the New York Public Library's Loie Fuller collection arranging a visit by Curie to Auguste Rodin, but gives no date and does not distinguish the Meudon villa from the Paris studio, and I could not confirm it against the archive. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from loie_fuller.journey.json, stop 'Meudon, the letter from Rodin'; auguste_rodin.journey.json carries no mention of Curie. Dated 1908 only to order the segment.
stops.campa: Loïe Fuller, who collects people the way other impresarios collect theatres, arranges for Marie Curie to be brought out to Auguste Rodin at Meudon. Rodin is the other man in France, along with Anatole France, whom Fuller names as having impressed her most. What passes between the sculptor and the physicist is not recorded by anyone who was in the room. Fuller's own memoir, published that year in Paris, keeps the two names in the same breath, and that is the whole of the evidence for the afternoon.
suggested_refs: Loie Fuller collection, New York Public Library, correspondence arranging a Curie visit to Rodin
loie_fuller.journey.json, stops 'Meudon, the letter from Rodin' and 'Paris, Quinze ans de ma vie'
sources: research dossier, Loïe Fuller section (not independently verified)

stops.name: Paris, the metal and the treatise
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1910 for both the isolation of metallic radium with André-Louis Debierne and the publication of the two-volume Traité de radioactivité by Gauthier-Villars; no day in the pool.
stops.campa: With André-Louis Debierne she electrolyses radium chloride over a mercury cathode and distils off the mercury, and what is left in the crucible is radium as a metal: brilliant white, and it tarnishes the moment air touches it. Twelve years after the element was announced from a spectral line, somebody has finally seen it. In the same year Gauthier-Villars publishes her Traité de radioactivité: two volumes, nine hundred and seventy pages, everything known about the subject, written by the person who opened it. She is forty-two.
suggested_refs: Marie Curie, Traité de radioactivité, 2 vols. (Paris: Gauthier-Villars, 1910)

segments.name: The Year of the Two Verdicts

stops.name: The Institut de France, the vote
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and for the loss to Édouard Branly. The margin is contested: the dossier says two votes, Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie' says the Academy 'failed, by one or two votes, to elect her.' The narrower claim is not made here.
stops.campa: She stands for the Académie des sciences. The campaign against her is run in the nationalist press and is about three things, none of them physics: that she is a woman, that she is a foreigner, and that she is Jewish, which she is not. On the twenty-third of January the Academy declines to elect her by one or two votes and takes Édouard Branly instead. She never stands again, and no woman is elected to the Academy for another fifty-one years. The doors of the Institut are guarded that day, and an usher on the step has his instructions: admit everyone except women.
suggested_refs: The Académie des sciences ballot of 23 January 1911, Branly 30 votes to Curie 28 in the reported tally

stops.name: Hotel Metropole, Brussels, the first Solvay
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Solvay Conference' gives the Hotel Metropole, Brussels, 30 October to 3 November 1911, with Curie among the attendees. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from einstein.journey.json, stop 'Brussels, the first Solvay Congress'; the geography lens's 50.8497/4.3547 is not used.
stops.campa: Twenty-four physicists are invited to Brussels by the industrialist Ernest Solvay to argue about radiation and the quantum. She is the only woman in the room and the only person present who has discovered an element. Albert Einstein meets her here for the first time and takes to her at once; they will write to each other until she dies. While the conference sits, Paris newspapers begin printing letters stolen from Paul Langevin's flat. By the time her train reaches the Gare du Nord there is a crowd outside her house.
suggested_refs: The group photograph of the first Solvay Congress, Brussels, November 1911
einstein.journey.json, stop 'Brussels, the first Solvay Congress'

stops.name: Paris, the letter from Loie Fuller
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The dossier cites a letter of 24 November 1911 from Loïe Fuller and quotes it; Wikipedia's article on Fuller records only that Curie was among those whose friendship Fuller's work attracted, and I could not reach the New York Public Library holding to confirm the letter or its wording. The research pool tagged it attested in both lenses and that tag is downgraded here. The pin is the canonical Paris coordinate, not a located address, because the letter's destination address is not in the pool.
stops.campa: Gustave Téry's paper prints the stolen letters in full. A mob gathers outside the house at Sceaux where her two daughters are, and stones go through the windows; she takes the children out to friends. Petitions circulate demanding that the foreign woman leave France, and colleagues write to advise her, gently, that she might consider leaving Paris until the thing dies down. Among the post of those weeks is a note from Loïe Fuller, who is a dancer, who has no advice to give, and who does not mention Langevin.
stops.quote: I love you and beg you to pay no attention to the lies.
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller to Marie Curie, letter of 24 November 1911, cited in the research dossier from the Loie Fuller collection, New York Public Library; not independently verified
suggested_refs: Loie Fuller collection, New York Public Library, correspondence with Marie Curie

stops.name: Stockholm, the second prize
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to her alone for the discovery of radium and polonium and the isolation of radium; the Nobel lecture, 'Radium and the New Concepts in Chemistry,' was delivered on 11 December 1911. Svante Arrhenius's letter urging her to stay away is carried in the dossier.
stops.campa: Svante Arrhenius writes to her from Stockholm advising her not to come: the scandal is in every paper, and the Academy would prefer that the prize be accepted by post. Nobody of either sex has yet held two Nobel Prizes. She answers that the prize was given for the discovery of radium and polonium, and that there is no connection whatever between her scientific work and her private life. Then she takes the train north with her sister Bronisława and her daughter Irène, and stands up in Stockholm to accept the chemistry prize herself.
suggested_refs: Marie Curie, Nobel Lecture, 'Radium and the New Concepts in Chemistry,' Stockholm, 11 December 1911
sources: nobelprize.org, Nobel lecture listing (via dossier source list)

stops.name: Norfolk Square, London, the assumed name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That Hertha Ayrton sheltered Curie in England in 1912, sometimes under an assumed name, is carried by the dossier; the specific address is Ayrton's documented London residence and is not independently confirmed for this stay. Dated to the year only.
stops.campa: She collapses after Stockholm: kidney surgery, a long convalescence, depression heavy enough that she cannot work for more than a year. Hertha Ayrton, an English physicist and suffragist who has fought the Royal Society over her own exclusion, takes her in and hides her, and for part of the stay Marie Curie is registered under a name that is not hers. In England nobody knows the face. She walks, and she does not go near a laboratory, and slowly the strength comes back.
stops.quote: Life is not easy for any of us. But what of that? We must have perseverance and above all confidence in ourselves.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Marie Curie, as quoted in Ève Curie, Madame Curie: A Biography (1937), trans. Vincent Sheean, part 2, p. 116; cited via Wikiquote and not confirmed against the book
suggested_refs: Hertha Ayrton's correspondence and household, Norfolk Square, London
sources: Wikiquote, Marie Curie (for the attributed line)

stops.name: Rue Pierre-et-Marie-Curie, the Institut du Radium
stops.date_confidence: attested: founded 1909 by the University of Paris and the Institut Pasteur, building completed 1914 (Wikipedia, 'Institut Curie'). Coordinate is the original 1914 laboratory at 1 rue Pierre et Marie Curie, now the Musée Curie, per OpenStreetMap; the pool's 48.8422/2.3427 was about 290 m off.
stops.campa: The laboratory she was promised in 1906 is finished at last, on a street the city has renamed for her husband and, while she is still alive, for her. It is built in two halves by two institutions that do not much like each other, physics under her and medicine under Claude Regaud, and she plants a garden of roses and lime trees in the courtyard between them. She hires women. Over the years the laboratory takes on researchers from Poland, Norway, Sweden, China, and India, and roughly a third of them are women.
stops.quote: I am among those who think that science has great beauty.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Marie Curie, as quoted in Ève Curie, Madame Curie: A Biography (1937), trans. Vincent Sheean, p. 341; cited via Wikiquote and not confirmed against the book
suggested_refs: The Musée Curie, 1 rue Pierre et Marie Curie, Paris, in the original 1914 laboratory building

stops.name: Bordeaux, the gram in a suitcase
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1914 in the dossier's 1913-1919 section; September is inferred from the German advance on Paris and the government's own removal to Bordeaux, and the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: The German army is at the Marne and the government has left Paris for Bordeaux. She puts France's entire stock of radium, one gram, into a lead-lined case weighing some twenty kilos, and carries it to the Gare d'Orsay herself, and sits with it on the train, and deposits it in a bank vault in Bordeaux. Then she looks for a room for the night, is told the hotels are full of ministers, and eventually gets a bed somewhere. She takes the first train back to Paris in the morning.
suggested_refs: The French national radium standard, prepared by Marie Curie in 1911 and evacuated in 1914

stops.name: The Marne, the cars with the generators
stops.date_confidence: attested for the programme, dated here to the first winter to order a stop that covers 1914-1918; the units moved constantly and no single site is documented, so the pin is a representative point in the Marne sector. Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie' gives 20 mobile radiological vehicles and 200 radiological units at field hospitals in the first year. The figure of 150 women trained as technicians comes from the dossier and is not in the encyclopaedia entry.
stops.campa: She learns anatomy. She learns to drive, and to change a tyre. Then she begs and borrows motor cars, fits each with an X-ray tube and a dynamo run off the engine, and sends them to the casualty stations. Twenty of them go out in the first year, and two hundred fixed installations behind them. The soldiers call the cars the petites Curies. She takes one herself with Irène, who is seventeen, and the two of them stand in field hospitals within range of the guns showing surgeons where the shrapnel is, hour after hour, unshielded.
suggested_refs: Marie Curie, La Radiologie et la guerre (Paris, 1921)

stops.name: Paris, the journalist who counts the radium
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1920 in the dossier's 1919-1924 section; month and day not recorded.
stops.campa: An American magazine editor, Marie Mattingly Meloney, waits a year for an interview and is finally shown into a bare office with two chairs. She asks what the laboratory most needs. She is told: a gram of radium, which costs a hundred thousand dollars, which the laboratory does not have and will not have, because the woman who discovered the element patented nothing and owns none of it. Meloney goes home and raises the hundred thousand dollars in small subscriptions from American women. What she sells them is not the physics. It is the widow in the black dress.
stops.quote: It must be done for itself, for the beauty of science, and then there is always the chance that a scientific discovery may become like the radium a benefit for humanity.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, 'The Discovery of Radium' (Vassar College lecture, 1921), Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Marie Curie Radium Fund, organized by Marie Mattingly Meloney, 1920-1921
sources: Marie Curie, 'The Discovery of Radium' (1921), Wikisource

stops.name: The White House, the key and the altered deed
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie', 1921 US tour). The honorary degrees taken during the tour are attested in general in the dossier; individual campuses, including Smith College and the Washington scientific receptions, are not itemized in the reachable sources and are not staged as stops here.
stops.campa: President Warren Harding hands her a small golden key at the White House, the deed to a gram of radium bought by the subscriptions of American women. She has read the deed the night before and found that it leaves the radium to her personally, and therefore to her daughters. She has refused to attend until a lawyer is fetched and the wording changed, so that the gram belongs to the laboratory and to whoever works in it after her. The ceremony proceeds with the corrected document. The tour that follows exhausts her; she cancels engagements, and Irène and Ève stand in for her.
suggested_refs: The 1921 deed of gift of one gram of radium, altered at Marie Curie's insistence to vest in the Institut du Radium

stops.name: Palais Wilson, Geneva, the committee on intellectual cooperation
stops.date_confidence: attested for her membership of the League of Nations' International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation from 1922, alongside Henri Bergson as inaugural chair, Albert Einstein, and Gilbert Murray. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from henri_bergson.journey.json, stop 'Palais Wilson, Geneva, the first chair of intellectual cooperation'; the geography lens gave 46.2136/6.1478, which is about 1.1 km south, and separately noted that from 1926 the committee's executive institute sat in Paris, so 'Geneva 1922-1934' overstates a single location.
stops.campa: The League of Nations assembles twelve people to keep the intellectual life of Europe from dividing again along the lines of the war. Henri Bergson takes the chair, Albert Einstein sits at the table, and Marie Curie is made vice-president. She argues for scholarships, for the protection of scientific property, for the right of a researcher to profit from a discovery, which is a position she has never taken for herself. She attends year after year, in a body with no budget and no power, and says afterwards that she believed in it.
suggested_refs: henri_bergson.journey.json, stop 'Palais Wilson, Geneva, the first chair of intellectual cooperation'
The International Institute of Intellectual Cooperation, Paris, from 1926

stops.name: Paris, the life of Pierre Curie
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1923 for the French publication of Pierre Curie; the English translation appeared bound with her own 'Autobiographical Notes' in 1923 in the United States and was reissued in 1932, which the pool carries as a reconstruction from bibliographic data.
stops.campa: Seventeen years after the rue Dauphine she writes his life. It is a short book and a plain one: the Curie family at Sceaux, the crystals, the shed, the accident in one paragraph. The same year, twelve years after the other Academy would not have her, the Académie nationale de médecine elects her a free associate, the first woman it has taken. Appended to the American edition of the book are her own autobiographical notes, written for the subscribers who bought her the radium. It is the only account of herself she ever gave.
suggested_refs: Marie Curie, Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes, trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg (Macmillan, 1923)

stops.name: Wawelska Street, the cornerstone
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1925 in the dossier's 1925-1933 section; month and day not recorded. Coordinate corrected to the Warsaw Radium Institute at ul. Wawelska 15 in Ochota, now the Maria Skłodowska-Curie National Research Institute of Oncology; the pool's 52.2247/21.0219 lay 2.6 km away in Śródmieście.
stops.campa: Poland exists again, and she lays the cornerstone of a radium institute in Warsaw. Her sister Bronisława, the doctor whose training she paid for out of a governess's wages forty years earlier, is running the project. The building is funded by public subscription: Poles buy bricks with their names on them, and the appeal is made in the name of a woman who left because there was nothing here for her to study. There is no money yet for radium to put in the building. She speaks in Polish.
suggested_refs: The Warsaw Radium Institute, ul. Wawelska 15, funded by public subscription from 1925

stops.name: Parc Leopold, Brussels, the fifth Solvay
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate inherited byte-identical from dirac.journey.json, stop 'Parc Leopold, Brussels, the Fifth Solvay Conference'.
stops.campa: Sixteen years after the first Solvay she is back in Brussels, in the front row of the photograph that becomes the most reproduced group portrait in the history of physics, seated next to Einstein. Seventeen of the twenty-nine people in the picture hold or will hold a Nobel Prize, and she is the only one in the frame with two. Behind and around her the argument has moved somewhere she cannot follow: the quantum has become a matter of probability and of what can be known at all, and the men debating it were children when she was boiling pitchblende.
suggested_refs: The group photograph of the Fifth Solvay Conference, Brussels, October 1927

stops.name: The White House, the second fund
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929 in the dossier's 1925-1933 section; month and day not recorded.
stops.campa: She crosses the Atlantic again, and Meloney has raised fifty thousand dollars again, and President Herbert Hoover hands it over. The money is not for Paris this time. It buys a gram of radium for Warsaw, for the institute on Wawelska Street that has walls and no source. She is sixty-one, and this is the last time she will cross an ocean. She stays at the White House as Hoover's guest, avoids the receptions where she can, sits for the photographers because Meloney has explained that the photographs are the fundraising, and goes home.
suggested_refs: The second Meloney campaign, 1929, and the purchase of radium for the Warsaw Radium Institute

stops.name: Wawelska Street, the institute opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1932 in the dossier's 1925-1933 section; month and day not recorded.
stops.campa: The Warsaw Radium Institute opens with Bronisława Dłuska as its director and her sister present at the ceremony. Marie Curie has paid for the radium and argued for the building, and she has lent it a name that in Poland is worth more than either. She does not run it and never will. The doctors on the staff address her in Polish, the language she was punished for using at school in this city, in a country whose universities had no place for her when she was fifteen. She is back at her desk in Paris within the week.
suggested_refs: The Warsaw Radium Institute under Bronisława Dłuska, from 1932

stops.name: The Institut du Radium, the daughter's element
stops.date_confidence: attested that Irène Curie and Frédéric Joliot discovered that light elements could be made radioactive by alpha bombardment, and that Enrico Fermi's Rome report of 25 March 1934 on neutron-induced radioactivity opens by crediting them (fermi.journey.json). The pool does not date the Joliot-Curie result itself, so the stop is dated to the year and placed at the laboratory where the work was done.
stops.campa: In her own laboratory, her daughter Irène and her son-in-law Frédéric Joliot bombard aluminium with alpha particles and find that the target goes on emitting after the source is taken away. They have made an element radioactive that was not. Marie Curie is shown the counter, takes the tube in her burned fingers, and looks at it for a long time. Within weeks the result is being built on in Rome, where Enrico Fermi opens his report on neutron-induced radioactivity by crediting the two of them by name.
stops.quote: It is my earnest desire that some of you should carry on this scientific work and keep for your ambition the determination to make a permanent contribution to science.
stops.quote_source: Marie Curie, 'The Discovery of Radium' (Vassar College lecture, 1921), Wikisource
suggested_refs: fermi.journey.json, stop 'Rome, the report of neutron-induced radioactivity'
The 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Irène Joliot-Curie and Frédéric Joliot

stops.name: Warsaw, the last visit
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1934 in the dossier's 1925-1933 section, with no month or day, so the date defaults to 01-01 and the stop is placed after the Paris laboratory stop on the reasonable order of travel rather than on a documented sequence. The pin is a general Warsaw coordinate.
stops.campa: She goes home to Poland for the last time. She is sixty-six, she cannot read a thermometer without glasses she keeps losing, her fingers are cracked and numb, and she has been anaemic for years without letting anyone measure how badly. No ceremony is recorded and no speech. She sees her sister, and the institute working, and the city she was born in, which is once again the capital of a country. Whether she knew this was the last time, and what month of the year it was, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Skłodowski family graves, Powązki Cemetery, Warsaw

stops.name: Sancellemoz, the marrow
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'). Coordinate corrected to the Sanatorium Sancellemoz at Praz Coutant, Passy, per OpenStreetMap; the pool's 45.9167/6.7 was a rounded valley point 2.8 km away. The attribution of the anaemia to cumulative exposure is later medical-historical consensus, not a finding on the death certificate, which records aplastic pernicious anemia.
stops.campa: She is taken by train to a sanatorium in the Haute-Savoie, above Passy, with a temperature and a blood count that has fallen through the floor. The diagnosis is aplastic pernicious anemia: the marrow has stopped making blood. She never wore a lead apron and did not think one necessary, and thirty-five years of radium and four years of unshielded X-ray tubes in field hospitals are what did it, though the certificate does not say so. She dies there on the fourth of July, aged sixty-six, in sight of the mountains.
suggested_refs: Sanatorium Sancellemoz, Praz Coutant, Passy, Haute-Savoie

stops.name: The cemetery at Sceaux, beside Pierre
stops.date_confidence: attested (dossier, Illness and Death). Coordinate corrected to the Cimetière de Sceaux on the rue Houdan per OpenStreetMap; the pool had reused the town hall coordinate, which would have stacked the burial on the wedding 500 m away.
stops.campa: They bury her at Sceaux on the sixth of July, in the grave where Pierre has been lying for twenty-eight years, in a ceremony with no priest and no speeches. No government is represented. Her brother Józef and her sister Bronisława each throw in a handful of soil brought from Poland. The family has told the press nothing and invited no official; the daughters and a few colleagues from the laboratory stand at the edge of the plot in the July heat while the gravediggers work. Almost nobody is there. It is over in a few minutes.
suggested_refs: The Curie family plot, Cimetière de Sceaux, rue Houdan

stops.name: The Pantheon, the lead lining
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'). Coordinate inherited byte-identical from victor_hugo.journey.json, stop 'Pantheon, the crypt'. The reported 1995 finding that the remains carried no dangerous radium contamination is carried by the dossier only and is not independently confirmed against an exhumation report.
stops.campa: Sixty-one years after Sceaux, President François Mitterrand and President Lech Wałęsa stand in the rue Soufflot while two coffins are carried up the steps of the Pantheon. She is the first woman put into that crypt for what she did rather than for whom she married. The remains are sealed in lead before reinterment. Measurements taken at the exhumation are reported to show no dangerous radium in the bones, which if true means the marrow was destroyed from outside, by the tubes and the gamma sources and the field hospitals, and not by anything she swallowed.

stops.name: The Bibliotheque nationale, the notebooks
stops.date_confidence: not an event. The Curie papers are a standing holding in the Manuscripts department of the BnF at the François-Mitterrand site; the reachable sources give no accession date, so the stop is dated to the present to place it last in the file. The afterlife lens placed the papers at Site Richelieu, which contradicts the BnF's own page and is corrected here.
stops.campa: Her laboratory notebooks from the 1890s are still radioactive. Radium-226 has a half-life near sixteen hundred years, and the popular telling turns that into a sealed vault and a signed waiver. What the library does is keep them in the manuscripts department, two on display after certified measurement and the rest consultable under a monitoring protocol, protected by plastic covers and not, whatever the story says, by lead. Ten minutes in front of the displayed pages costs a visitor about two nanosieverts, some five thousand times less than a day spent standing outdoors.
suggested_refs: bnf.fr, 'Les cahiers de Marie Curie conservés à la BnF sont-ils radioactifs ?'
